description: We are Mubeen and Hassan, full-stack engineers building a crop rotation tool using NASA Earth data (POWER, SMAP) and soil metrics. We provide strong frontend, backend, and API architecture. We are looking for teammates with skills in GIS/remote sensing, agronomy, or UI/UX and pitching. We have a clear technical plan and are ready to execute—DM us to team up and build!
summary:
Choosing what to plant next is becoming harder as rainfall, heat, and water availability change. We built Rotation Atlas to help farmers explore their options and understand the trade-offs before changing their crop rotation.

Our prototype uses NASA POWER weather observations in an Iowa case study to compare four crop rotations over a 12-year planning period, including the existing rotation. Farmers can explore how different assumptions affect the comparison, review the evidence behind the results, and export a report for discussion with an agricultural adviser. The tool also makes uncertainty and missing data visible, so users can judge how much confidence to place in the results.

Rotation Atlas addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA data into a practical starting point for crop-rotation decisions. It helps farmers weigh possible changes while keeping their experience, priorities, and local knowledge at the center of the decision.
details:
Rotation Atlas helps farmers explore a practical question: “What could I plant next, and what would I be trading off?” A rotation may offer more soil cover but cost more to establish. A forage crop may look promising on paper but be difficult to justify without the right equipment or a nearby buyer. We built the project around those everyday decisions.

Our current prototype focuses on an Iowa case study. It compares four strategies: the existing maize–soybean rotation, a version with a rye cover crop, a more diverse rotation with wheat and clover, and a longer rotation that includes oats and alfalfa. Farmers can review these options side by side and adjust their priorities around water demand, living soil cover, and gross margin.

The comparison uses daily NASA POWER weather observations from 2013–2024. We divide that record into three four-year weather blocks and replay each strategy under the same conditions over a shared four-year planning horizon. This gives farmers a way to explore how an option behaves across different historical conditions. These are scenarios, rather than forecasts of future weather or guaranteed farm outcomes.

Behind the interface, a daily water-balance model estimates soil-water availability, crop water demand, and irrigation use. Crop assumptions and illustrative enterprise budgets support comparisons of gross margin, while crop calendars show periods with living cover. Users can change rainfall, temperature, prices, soil-water capacity, and management assumptions to see how sensitive the results are.

We also ask about practical constraints: available labor, operating budget, irrigation access, machinery, crop suitability, and confirmed buyers. An unanswered question stays marked as unknown. If feasibility remains unresolved, the tool withholds an overall preference and highlights what needs checking. Farmers can record their own choice, save notes, export the decision record, or defer the decision until they have spoken with a local adviser.

The creative part of Rotation Atlas is bringing environmental evidence, farm economics, and practical feasibility into the same conversation. Instead of stopping at a crop score, it helps users ask why an option looks promising, what assumptions support it, and what new information could change the comparison.

We developed the application using TypeScript, React, Next.js, and CSS, with a Node.js runtime. Python scripts support NASA data capture and evidence processing, and Vitest supports automated testing of the comparison logic. A packaged weather dataset also allows the core demonstration to run offline without a live data download.

Throughout development, we considered usability, limited connectivity, differences between regional weather observations and field conditions, and the risk of presenting estimates with too much confidence. The prototype has not yet been validated against independent field outcomes, and it does not claim measured improvements in soil carbon, erosion, or pest control.

Our intended impact is to make crop-rotation planning easier to discuss and investigate. We want farmers and agricultural advisers to have a clearer starting point for weighing options, identifying missing evidence, and deciding what deserves a closer look on their own land.
